units.text: We'll pick the first evidence and safest next action for an incident. A latency spike calls for a trace and latency evidence; missing logs call for checking the collection path. Different symptoms point to different first checks.
After a scoped action, check service health and the user-facing objective. If the result worsens, pause and follow the agreed recovery action rather than continuing a rollout that isn't working.
Ask whether it is getting worse, what happened in a particular request, or where time went. Use a metric for trends, logs for recorded events, and a trace for the path through dependencies.

Use Session Manager for authorized interactive access, Run Command for a bounded one-time task, State Manager for a desired configuration, and Automation to coordinate steps and approvals. Keep the scope as narrow as the operation permits.

Map the symptom to the likely boundary before acting. If the queue is backing up, distinguish worker capacity from a repeatedly failing message. Look at queue age and errors first. Then check whether the chosen action improves the customer outcome.

We'll trace a bill back to the architecture that produced it. The demand curve drives choices about compute, storage and network traffic. Each choice can create different usage dimensions. Optimize what the workload actually needs without losing its resilience or service target.

Compute Savings Plans can cover eligible usage across E C two, Fargate and Lambda. E C two Instance Savings Plans trade flexibility for a given instance family and Region. Reserved Instances follow their own scope and attributes. Compare the eligible steady usage before choosing a commitment.

Savings Plans reduce eligible prices; they do not reserve E C two capacity. An On-Demand Capacity Reservation can hold capacity in a specific Availability Zone and doesn't inherently give a discount. Check each requirement independently before assuming one purchase solves both.

Use Spot for retryable work with checkpoints and diversify capacity. Interruption notice can help a worker exit safely but is not a promise it will finish. Keep the interruption-sensitive baseline on a suitable capacity option and verify the backlog can recover.

We'll reduce idle capacity before committing to it. Collect memory and C P U as appropriate, consider recommendations, then benchmark a candidate under production-like load. A smaller instance that misses the target is not a good saving.

For variable traffic, use a target tracking signal that follows demand. For predictable peaks, schedule capacity ahead. Keep a minimum where availability requires it. Compare the resulting capacity and user experience instead of judging only average utilization.

E C two provides instance control, Fargate runs containers without managing hosts, and Lambda fits supported event-driven handlers. Step Functions coordinates work instead of replacing compute. Choose Standard or Express by execution requirements, then account for how the chosen mode is billed.

For inference, estimate actual input and output tokens and evaluate a model that meets quality. Batching can suit asynchronous work; provisioned throughput suits eligible traffic patterns only if the cost works. An application response cache differs from model prompt caching. Verify savings and data boundaries.

We'll see which path the request actually takes. A cache hit means the viewer gets the object without another origin request. When a request misses the edge cache, Origin Shield can provide another shared cache layer. Compare its cost and the origin work it avoids.

Draw the actual path before estimating transfer. Crossing Availability Zones, crossing Regions and leaving A W S can have different rules. nat, Transit Gateway and interface endpoints may also add processing charges. Check the specific services and directions rather than applying one rate to every hop.

Keep routine dependent traffic local where the architecture supports it. But if the service needs to survive an Availability Zone loss, keep an approved cross-zone design. Separate application transfer from managed replication charges and check pricing for the specific service.

We'll choose private-subnet egress by destination. A supported S three or Dynamo D B gateway endpoint uses its service prefix list and endpoint target. An interface endpoint serves eligible private services. Use a suitable nat path for general public I P version four egress if required.

Compare any hourly and data-processing charges for the relevant path. A gateway endpoint has no additional endpoint charge, but other service charges can still apply. Verify routing, endpoint policy and the intended destination.

Transit Gateway connects networks and carries routed traffic. PrivateLink gives a consumer private access to a supported service. Compare attachments and data processing for Transit Gateway with endpoint time and data processing for PrivateLink under the actual topology.

Set the recovery point and recovery time objectives before choosing what goes to another Region. Compare the S three and database replication examples by actual replication, storage and transfer. A second Region only helps if the application can recover within its requirements there.

The diagram shows an application directly calling a different Region. Check that network path for possible transfer charges. Bedrock-managed cross-Region inference profiles are a separate case: A W S does not add a routing or data-transfer surcharge for the managed routing itself.

Even when managed routing has no surcharge, verify eligible destination Regions, residency and latency. Model inference usage still has its own price. Other traffic in the architecture must be evaluated separately.
